senses: An exaggerated facial expression consisting of flushed cheeks, rolled-back eyes, and the tongue hanging out, intended to depict a person having an orgasm.
ety: From Japanese アヘ顔(がお) (ahegao), from アヘアヘ (aheahe, “panting”) + 顔(かお) (kao, “face”).
examples: During the set of intercourse at the end of the story, Sherlock is also drawn featuring ahegao expressions, frequently used in hentai or pornographic works.
Without anime I would never have been introduced to such thought provoking concepts as ahegao or 15 year old girls with boobs the size of basketballs.
In addition to standard cosplay and PG-13, NSFW pictures, she also became known for her ahegao — facial expressions meant to mimic the orgasms of hentai characters.

senses: To make a noise like something moving quickly through the air.
To throw with a rapid slamming motion.
To slice, especially into large pieces; to chop.
ety: Imitative. Compare wang.
examples: The holder of the torch grunted, and (after pausing a second at B.'s bed to inspect a picture of perfect innocence) banged out through the door which whanged to behind him...
I don't know how long it might have gone on if Grandfather hadn't lost his temper. He swung the bridle up over his head and whanged it down across the buckskin's rump.

senses: The seizure of someone's property by force; pillage; plunder.
ety: From Middle English rapyne, from Old French rapine, from Latin rapīna, from rapiō. Doublet of ravine.
examples: Good Rapine, stab him: he is a ravisher.

The Bat—they called him the Bat. Like a bat he chose the night hours for his work of rapine; like a bat he struck and vanished, pouncingly, noiselessly; like a bat he never showed himself to the face of the day.

senses: A brandy distilled from white wine in the region around Cognac in France.
A dark orangish brown color.
ety: Borrowed from French cognac, from Cognac, a city in France, from Medieval Latin Comniacum, from the name Cominius + Gallo-Roman suffix -acum, from Proto-Celtic *-ākom.
examples: Major manufacturers add a small proportion of caramel to color their cognacs.
Cognac, with the addition of a little paprika and the yolk of an egg, is considered an effective aphrodisiac aid.
We’d have a script meeting for the next day’s shooting that lasted until two in the morning, and he’d be up again at six for a breakfast meeting. I survived on cognac. I have no idea how he did it.

senses: Sloppy, hasty, shoddy, or inelegant.
ety: From kludge + -y.
examples: This is kind of a kludgy solution, but it will work for now.
What is still kludgy is how the data is gathered and passed to the function InjectHTML.

senses: A female author.
ety: From Middle English aucteuresse; equivalent to author + -ess.
examples: Eve was the authoress of sin, Mary the authoress of merit… the one wounded, the other healed.
He understands those things, and he says it's a remarkable piece of work. But are you fancying she's an authoress?—not a bit of it.

senses: An anticapitalist skinhead.
ety: From red + skin, from skinhead.
examples: The Red & Anarchist Skinheads, a left‐wing splinter of the SHARP group, formed in 1993. It grew out of influences from the redskin culture in England.

senses: A levitating board that can be ridden in the manner of a surfboard or skateboard.
A small self-balancing two-wheeled motorised vehicle, related to a scooter.
ety: From hover + board, patterned off of skateboard. First mentioned in the 1989 film Back to the Future Part II.
examples: Northern introduced a ban on e-scooters, hoverboards and e-skateboards on all its stations and trains from December 1, because of a fire risk. Electric wheelchairs and bikes are exempt.

senses: The condition of having unkempt hair, generally as a result of having just woken up from sleep.
ety: From bed + head. Superficially similar to, but etymologically distinguishable from, forms built from -head.
examples: She always came to the office late because she was an INSOMNIAC, lewd grin, bedhead, and miniskirt, the CEO laughing his head off down the hallway, old word style, but new to have this dirty kind of hilarious brunette.

senses: To fill to satisfaction; to satisfy.
To satisfy to excess. To fill to satiety.
ety: First attested in the 1440–1450s, in Middle English; borrowed from Latin satiātus, perfect passive participle of satiō (“to fill full, satiate, satisfy”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from satis (“sufficient”).
examples: Nothing seemed to satiate her desire for knowledge.

senses: Designed to resemble a handwriting style developed in Italy in the 16th century.
Having letters that slant or lean to the right; oblique.
ety: Named after the nation of Italy, as it was first used by an Italian printer, Aldo Manuzio, around 1500. Literally Italy + -ic.
examples: The text was impossible to read: every other word was underlined or in a bold or italic font.

senses: Subtitles translated by amateurs.
Translation of subtitles by amateurs.
ety: Short for fan subtitle.
examples: In the case of fansub, the danmaku interface effectively visualizes and mediates the cosmopolitan contact zone as a layer of paratextual comments on screen (Fig 8.5).

senses: The amount that a spoon will hold, either level or heaped.
ety: From Middle English sponeful, sponefull, sponful, spone-ful, equivalent to spoon + -ful.
examples: Martin roused himself and sat up and began to eat, between spoonfuls reassuring Maria that he had not been talking in his sleep and that he did not have any fever.

senses: The act of defiling.
ety: From defile + -ment.
examples: The new law also applies to acts of defilement besides burning, such as publicly ripping a flag up. Public display of the Nazi swastika and other Nazi symbols is already banned in Germany.

senses: Religious practice that focuses on morality while placing little emphasis on doctrine or the metaphysical; adherence to a system of morality with little or no reference to religion.
ety: From French moralisme.
examples: The scientific superiority of liberal theology, it is now said, is indeed incontestable, but its theological position is weak, for its moralism and humanism lack insight into the dæmonic character of human existence.

senses: A preliminary model or sketch used in preparation for making a sculpture.
ety: Borrowed from French maquette.
examples: His presence would be an affront to my body; so, for it, there would be the rare delight of extinguishing an imperfect and distressed version of itself, a prototype, a maquette.

senses: In Ancient Egypt, a figurine of a dead person, placed in their tomb to do their work for them in the afterlife.
ety: Borrowed from Egyptian w-S-b-t:y-A53 (wšbtj, “ushabti”, literally “answerer”), by folk etymology from earlier SA-wA-b-t:y-A53 (šꜣwꜣbtj), perhaps from S-wA-b-M1 (šwꜣb, “persea (tree)”), which may have been the material they were originally made from. The variant forms shawabti, shabti are borrowed directly from the earlier Egyptian forms šꜣwꜣbtj and šꜣbtj, respectively.
examples: The air was all at once full of Egyptian and Greek tear-bottles, Ushabti, and Sèvres.

senses: To pour off (a liquid) gently, so as not to disturb the sediment.
To pour from its original vessel into one intended for a different use or appearance.
To remove (a clone or other artificially-gestated baby) from its chamber, vat, or artificial womb.
To rehouse people while their buildings are being refurbished or rebuilt.
ety: From French décanter, from Medieval Latin dēcanthāre, from dē- + canthus (“beak of a cup or jug”).
examples: After washing, the insoluble lime soap is decomposed with hot dilute sulphuric acid. The melted fatty acids thus rise as an oil to the surface, when they are decanted.

senses: A whitish sebaceous secretion that collects between the glans penis and foreskin or in the vulva.
ety: From Latin, borrowed from Ancient Greek σμῆγμα (smêgma), alternative form of σμῆμα (smêma, “soap, detergent”), from σμάω (smáō, “to wipe, clean”).
examples: I saw Mrs St Cloud wander happily through the flower-filled streets, her belly smeared with smegma, breasts bruised by the hands of boys.

senses: Not ascertained; uncertain; undetermined; unknown.
ety: From un- + ascertained.
examples: Throughout all future time, as now, the human mind may occupy itself, not only with ascertained phenomena and their relations, but also with that unascertained something which phenomena and their relations imply.
A conjecture vaguely taking shape in his mind resolved itself to nothing again, and left him with only the ache of something unascertained.

senses: A chisel with a sharp point, used for engraving; a graver.
A prehistoric flint tool
ety: From French burin. Doublet of boline.
examples: I kept staring at the same wallpaper on the same wall; I stared at it so often that every line of its zigzag pattern has etched itself on the innermost folds of my brain as if with an engraver’s burin.

senses: Prone to or capable of having orgasms.
Very exciting or stimulating.
ety: From Ancient Greek. The historically "correct" form is orgastic. Nouns from Ancient Greek that end in -sm regularly form adjectives ending in -stic: for example, enthusiasm / enthusiastic, sarcasm / sarcastic. By way of counterexample, the ahistorical -mic also appears in the terms protoplasmic and cataclysmic (instead of *protoplastic and *cataclystic).
examples: Seemingly every year, another study announces that married women are more orgasmic than single women.

They've helped non-orgasmic women become orgasmic, they've helped orgasmic women become more orgasmic, and they've helped many women experience their first multiple orgasms (we'll talk about that later!).
The gentler the sensation or touch the more orgasmic I am.

senses: A capped double-reed instrument.
A buzzing insect.
Police officer.
Anything that produces a buzzing sensation.
ety: From buzz + -ie.
examples: The brilliant qualities of the Diritto and the Curvo seem to lend themselves to use with sackbutts or large mixed ensembles composed of "buzzies" such as shawms, racketts, and crumhorns.
But be they flies or be they wasps, I neither care for buzzies nor stings.

Sue had climbed up to the rafters and attached her mosquito netting over one of the exposed beams in the ceiling, and Edgar had climbed into the bed under it so no flying buzzies would mess with his ears.

senses: Of birds: sitting persistently and protectively on a nest, in order to hatch eggs.
Of any creature or person: showing an interest in raising young.
Brooding, dwelling upon one's thoughts; moody.
ety: From Middle English *brody, *brodi, from Old English brōdiġ (“broody”), equivalent to brood + -y. Cognate with German brütig (“broody”).
examples: He didn't even give me one of his broody looks that gave nothing away about his thoughts at all (except the fact he was broody). He gave me a look I'd never seen on him before. A remorseful one.
Peter's doubt in his own leadership grew like fungus on his thoughts. He became broody and snapped at people. He was finding himself more and more behind a closed door. He just needed a break.
He could be a little broody at times, especially when his thoughts were focused on school, class, a project, or hunting. That's just the way he was.

senses: To coax (a rabbit) from a burrow by poking a stick down the hole and moving it about; to delve into a hole in order to locate an animal.
To poke around a hole with a stick, as to explore, remove obstacles, etc.
ety: British dialect (Hertfordshire, Essex), from pug (“to poke”) + -le (“frequentative suffix”).
examples: He puggled around in the oil cavity with his little lead pencil until it slipped out of his fingers and went down into the oil cavity.

senses: Concise and meaningful.
Of, like, or abounding in pith; spongy or having small holes or pits.
ety: From Middle English pithy, pythy, equivalent to pith + -y.
examples: The following passage, which is exquisitely pithy and exquisitely modest, winds up the description:- "In this apparatus there is nothing new but its simplicity and thorough trustworthiness."
IT was a pithy saying that of Lorenzo de' Medici, and true as pithy, that we are enjoined to forgive our enemies, but nowhere are we told that we should forgive our friends.

senses: Any debris or fragments of disintegrated material.
Rock consisting of accumulated debris from decayed rocks, like sand, that often is joined by cement.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin dētrītus (“(that which is) rubbed away”), from dēterō (“rub away”).
examples: But of course: no clutter. No newspapers, no renegade scraps of domestic detritus, no rubber bands, paper clips, coupons, pens or pencils, notebooks, magazines. No knives. Where were the knives?

The cutting head removes any chips out of the railhead and restores the required surface shape. The trains also clear up their own detritus as they travel. Neither milling chips nor grinding dust remain on the track.

senses: Meat or fish that has been scored and broiled.
ety: The noun is derived from Spanish carbonada (“carbonized”) (from carbonar (“to carbonize”)) + -ado (suffix forming past participles of regular verbs ending in -ar). Carbonada appears to have been modelled after Italian carbonata (“coal pile; stew of beef in red wine”), from carbone (“coal; charcoal”) (from Latin carbō (“coal; charcoal”), from Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“to burn”)) + -ata. The verb is derived from the noun.
examples: The carbonadoes consisted of any meat scotched on both sides and sprinkled with seasonings in various combinations, and then either broiled over the fire or before it.

senses: shimmering, or shining with a faint, or intermittent or trembling gleam or light.
(Apparently) shaking or trembling.
ety: From shimmer + -y (suffix meaning ‘inclined to’ forming adjectives).
examples: There will always be something worth living for while there are shimmery afternoons.
The length of the gorge on both sides was hung as it were with black shimmery velvet curtains, and Mowgli sank as he looked, for those were the clotted millions of the sleeping bees.
The tall girl is the shimmeriest, lips painted the color of the inside of an oyster shell, eyelids swirled in mother-of-pearl.

senses: The quality of being exuberant; cheerful or vigorous enthusiasm; liveliness.
An instance of exuberant behaviour.
An overflowing quantity; superfluousness.
An abundance of wealth.
ety: From French exubérance, from Latin exuberantia (“superabundance”), from exuberare (“to grow thickly, to abound”); from ex- (“out”) + uber (“udder”), which would have originally referred to a cow or she-goat which was making so much milk that it naturally dripped or sprayed from the udder.
examples: Tottenham's desire for a win against a Norwich side playing with energy and exuberance made for an enthralling, end-to-end game.

senses: A feather or plume, or feather-shaped item, used as an adornment or ornament, typically in hats or hair.
The feathery crown of some seeds (such as the dandelion).
ety: Borrowed from French aigrette (“egret”). Doublet of egret.
examples: She was formal in manner, and made calls in rustling, steel-gray brocades and a tall bonnet with bristling aigrettes.

Young women attired often in nothing more than ostrich-feather aigrettes dyed in colors of doubtful taste ran nubilely up and down the marble staircases, chased by young men in razor-toed ball shoes of patent-leather.

senses: Vaccinium myrtillus, the wild European blueberry of the cowberry family.
The shrub of the above-mentioned plant.
ety: Probably of North Germanic origin (Danish bøllebær), from Old Norse bolli (Proto-Germanic *bullǭ) + ber.
examples: Among the pines grew rowans hung with scarlet berries, and bilberry bushes whose leaves would be fair game for white moth caterpillars in spring.

senses: A functionary of lower rank than a herald, but discharging similar duties; an attendant of the heralds, e.g. in the College of Arms.
A Grand Lodge Officer who guards the inner door during a meeting of the Grand Lodge.
A royal messenger, (particularly) one with the authority to execute warrants.
A warrant officer.
ety: From Middle English pursevant et al., from Old French pursuivant, present participle of pursuivre (“to follow”). Doublet of pursuant.
examples: The herald Hope, forerunning Fear, / And Fear, the pursuivant of Hope.

senses: Unimportant or insubstantial talk, events, or actions; drivel.
The idle rich.
Highly speculative investment.
ety: From Middle English froth, frooth, froþ, likely a borrowing from Old Norse froða, from Proto-Germanic *fruþǭ; Old English āfrēoþan (“to foam, froth”) is from same Germanic root. Verb attested from late 14th century. Compare Swedish fradga.
examples: Thousands of African children die each day: why do the newspapers continue to discuss unnecessary showbiz froth?
The discussion at the conference was mostly froth and posturing.

But is it possible for those who speak of God promiscuously and at random, is it possible that they should utter his Name with reverence, when all the rest of the Discourse is nothing but Froth and Levity?

senses: A weaned piglet; any piglet.
ety: From Middle English schote, of uncertain origin. Perhaps a special use of Middle English schote (“projectile, young shoot”), or perhaps of Middle Low German origin, cognate with West Flemish schote (“young piglet”).
examples: There would have been nature studies – a tiger pursuing a bird of paradise, a choking snake sheathing whole the flayed trunk of a shoat.

senses: Marked by inclusiveness.
ety: From inclusion + -ary.
examples: His moderate, inclusionary vision is in keeping with our values.

senses: A carriage; a vehicle, now chiefly in French contexts.
ety: Borrowed from French voiture, from Latin vectūra. Doublet of vecture and vettura.
examples: When the voiture stopped in the village, there seemed to be a nonplusation, to coin a word for the nonce, between my friend and his sisters.

senses: A Mexican dish made by wrapping a filling in a tortilla, then baking in a sauce.
ety: From Spanish enchilada, past participle of enchilar (“to add chili pepper to”).
examples: It was a nice little pub in the middle of nowhere / Anywhere would have been better / I ordered enchiladas and I ate 'em

senses: Living again; brought back to life.
ety: Borrowed from Latin redivīvus.
examples: A tall, athletic, tanned man, his smooth black hair slick with oil, long sideburns, neatly trimmed moustache, Clark Gable redivivus.

senses: A person, usually a Muslim woman, who wears a hijab.
ety: From hijab + -i.
examples: The findings and implications of this study have been categorized into themes in order to illustrate the essence of how hijabi youth experience social activities in Ottawa secondary schools.
Almost all hijabis I encountered—except Intisar, Elizabeth, Sharmila, and Muna—were chic hijabis typically garbed in attractive, elegant, yet modest ensembles.
